CF1's only claim about that path is its near-term floor and its direction: the moat is protectable for $5k–$25k today, there is no near-term revenue, and every step toward the end product is gated on S2 closing and funded by option / government / buyer money (the spending rule, CF1.4) — never on founder cash chasing the dream, and never by selling the moat.

CF1.3 Why hardware / a physical source is premature — the blocker is source/energy closure

The single most important commercial decision in Part 0 is a negative one: do not build a physical device, a source, or any hardware first. This is not caution for its own sake — it is forced by the document's own results, and it is the commercial reading of the two gating gaps in Part L (§L0.3): source (HC-02) and energy (HC-03).

The argument is short and fail-closed:

  1. The current blocker is not engineering — it is source/energy closure. G1, the deepest exemplar, carries a genuine invariant forward-distance deficit and still terminates at FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC (HC-02): declared vacuum, yet T_eff = G_μν/8π ≠ 0, a 100% source mismatch, with the deeper root cause that the deficit needs ρ_eff = −8.038×10⁻⁶ < 0 — an exotic negative energy density that no admissible field in S_eff supplies (HC-03). Every textbook warp metric (G2: Alcubierre, Natário, Van Den Broeck) fails the same energy gate. There is nothing to source the device with; the thing a physical source would have to produce is the exact thing the document has shown is, as yet, unsourced and exotic.
  2. Therefore hardware is the wrong unit of work at this rung. Building a physical source before source/energy closure exists would be building an apparatus for a profile the platform itself cannot yet source — the literal FAIL_HIDDEN_EXOTICITY / FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC failure mode, embodied in metal. It would also breach the Part L scope boundary (§L0.8): Part L "does not provide instructions for building high-energy sources, beam systems, reactors, radiation systems, weaponizable systems, or flight hardware."
  3. CIPs fire only when the closure artifact exists. This is the operational rule of Part L (§L0.2.3), carried verbatim and never weakened: CIPs are filed ONLY when the corresponding closure artifact exists — no source-ledger CIP (IP-2) without a real SourceMatchReport; no observability CIP (IP-4) without a null-controlled signal model; no future physical-embodiment filing (IP-12) without independent evidence. The commercial corollary is exact: if you may not even file a CIP on a physical embodiment until an independent lab observable exists, you certainly may not spend cash building that embodiment first. IP-12 (future physical-embodiment filings) sits at the top of the IP ladder, reserved for BRL-6+, behind independent evidence — it is the last thing funded, not the first.

So the premise "build the device first" is foreclosed three ways at once: by the physics (source/energy is open and exotic), by the scope boundary (no hardware content), and by the IP rule (no embodiment filing — let alone embodiment spend — without an independent artifact). The moat inverts all three: it is the asset that exists at BRL-2, costs $5k–$25k to protect, files only the front-loadable IP (IP-0, IP-1, IP-7, IP-8, IP-9 — all of which protect the method, not any drive), and is the option value that may later justify funding a test of source/energy closure under a frozen milestone. The end product that an eventual S2 closure would enable is sold B2C or to government — never the method itself. Hardware is not banned forever; it is sequenced last, behind every artifact gate — and the protected moat is what preserves the right to even get there.

CF1.4 The model and the spending rule — protect the moat, prove the physics, then sell the end product

The commercial thesis is a three-verb sequence, and the order is the discipline:

THE MODEL
  PROTECT the moat       — IP-0/IP-1/IP-7/IP-8/IP-9 over the native-geometry method (front-loaded;
                           no CIPs yet); the method is NEVER sold or licensed              [≤ $25k EST]
  PROVE the physics      — close S2 (source/energy) under the frozen Part-L milestone

  SELL the END PRODUCT   — only after S2 closes: a finished end product sold B2C (consumer) or to a
                           government buyer — the buyer purchases the PRODUCT, never the method

The gated path (the canonical sequence for Part P): protect the moat → option / government-funded validation sprint → close S2 (artifact-backed CIPs fire only as artifacts appear) → end product sold B2C or to government. Read it against Part L: the middle steps are exactly the Part-L instruments — the funded sprint is the §L0.5 90-day hostile validation sprint; the artifact-backed CIPs are IP-2…IP-6 fired only when their artifacts exist (§L0.2.3); and the option → convert structure is the strategic-acquirer / government option→validate→convert logic (§L0.6, IP-10 → IP-11). The end-product sale is the terminal state, reachable only through the S2 gate — there is no near-term product revenue and no route that sells the moat to fund the sprint.

The spending rule (the hard cash-discipline of Part P, a FOUNDER guideline, not financial advice):

Self-fund only $10k–$50k maximum — and only on moat protection — then require option money, a government program, or a buyer to fund any deeper physics validation.

This is the cash-flow analogue of the fail-closed gate ladder. Just as a candidate cannot self-promote past a gate it has not cleared, the founder cannot self-fund past $10k–$50k and cannot self-fund the physics at all. Past that ceiling, the next dollar must come from option money, a government program, or a buyer — never from the founder chasing closure on conviction, and never from selling the method. The serious 90-day sprint ($150k–$350k FOUNDER ESTIMATE) and the acquirer-grade external sprint ($500k–$1.5M+ FOUNDER ESTIMATE) sit above this ceiling by design: they are funded externally, not by the founder's savings. The rule is what keeps the whole enterprise from becoming the very thing the document exists to screen out — an unsourced claim funded past its evidence.

Patent cash-discipline (factual fees + estimated attorney costs; verify before filing; not legal advice). The front-loadable IP that protects the moat is cheap relative to its protective value. The USPTO provisional filing fee is $325 (regular entity) / $130 (small entity) / $65 (micro entity)** — *verify the current fee schedule before filing*, as fees change. The dominant cost for a software provisional is **not** the government fee but **attorney/prep**: a **FOUNDER ESTIMATE of ~$6,000 for preparation plus filing and drawing costs, with complex cases varying widely. The discipline that keeps this honest is Part L's operational rule again: IP-0 (notebook/hashes) and IP-1 (base provisional) are filed now, to establish priority over the native-geometry method; the CIPs (IP-2…IP-6) cost nothing yet because none of their closure artifacts exist — and filing one before its artifact is a FORBIDDEN_PROMOTION, not a milestone (§L1.6 invariant IP_FILING_IS_ARTIFACT_BACKED). The cash exposure of "protect the moat" is therefore bounded to a provisional plus front-loaded software copyright and trade-secret hygiene — well inside the $10k–$50k self-fund ceiling — with every expensive, embodiment-shaped filing deferred behind an artifact that does not yet exist.

CF1.5 How CF1 anchors to Part L — the option→validate→convert logic, restated commercially

CF1 is the commercial precondition for Part L's deal, and it must never weaken Part L's buyer logic. The single most important sentence of Part L (§L0.6) is carried here unchanged: a strategic Mars-transport-scale acquirer (or a government buyer) should not buy "a claimed engine"; it should option the IP (IP-10), fund a frozen 90-day hostile validation sprint (§L0.5), and convert (IP-11) only if the frozen BRL-4 / M1_EFT_CANDIDATE milestone is hit and an independent hostile review accepts it.

The commercial reading is the on-ramp to that ask. The protected moat does three things, none of which touch the physics ceiling and none of which involve selling the method:

  • It keeps the founder at BRL-2-and-stable without dilution or overclaim — the native-geometry method, the negative-control corpus, and the front-loaded IP (IP-0/IP-1/IP-7/IP-8/IP-9) are protected for ≤ $25k, not financed by selling a stake in a dream and not by renting out the screen.
  • It makes the option cheap and rational for the buyer, because the asset offered is "the protected native-geometry method plus the right to file CIPs as evidence accrues," which already has standalone option value as a defensible moat. The moat is the floor of the deal — a real, IP-protected asset that no competitor can practice, not a consolation prize.
  • It keeps the conversion honest, because the path to deeper physics is gated by the spending rule (CF1.4) and the milestone (§L0.5), not by founder burn. The dream is tested with option / government / buyer money against a frozen predicate — never assumed, never self-funded past the ceiling, never funded by selling the moat.

Stated as the asymmetry Part L already proves: even the expected outcome — every candidate fails — leaves the acquirer (and the founder) owning a rigorous, IP-protected native-geometry method that no one else can practice. CF1 adds the missing commercial fact: that moat is protectable today as option value, which is what carries the founder to the option conversation without ever selling the method — and the only revenue the strategy ever points at is a B2C-or-government end product, gated on S2 closing. There is no route in CF1 — as there is none in Part L (§L0.6) — from a "no" on any clause to "we built the device anyway," and no route that sells the moat to anyone.

CF2 — The Cash-Flow Ladder and the Lowest-Burn Path to the End Product

Closure status: 1 TOY_DEFINED (ceiling PASS_TOY; this is a Part P commercial-strategy leaf — it promotes no candidate, presents no new computational result, and crosses no physics gate) · Default mode status: TOY_MODEL/AUDIT · Buildability standing: approximately BRL-2 (validated negative-control corpus), with a defined path to test for BRL-4 (EFT_CANDIDATE under the frozen milestone) · Scope: founder cash-flow sequencing toward a gated B2C/government end product, mapped onto the Part L BRL and IP ladders; NOT a hardware-construction manual, NOT financial advice, NOT legal advice. All dollar figures below are FOUNDER ESTIMATES, not guarantees, and there is no near-term product revenue.

CF2.0 What this chapter is, and the one rule it serves

Chapter CF1 stated the thesis. This chapter prices it. The thesis, carried exactly and never weakened anywhere below: do not build a physical device first, and do not sell the method. The patented native-geometry method/system is the protected moat, never licensed or sold as software to anyone. The revenue endgame is a single end product sold B2C (consumer) or to a government buyer — the buyer purchases the product, never the method — and that end product is gated on the S2 source/energy physics closing, which is the open barrier. In the words of the model this whole Part P is built around: "Protect the moat, prove the physics (close S2), then sell the end product B2C or to government."

CF2 takes that one-line model and turns it into two operational objects a founder can actually act on:

  1. The cash-flow ladder (CF2.2) — five rungs of founder cash needed per goal, from "protect the moat" at the bottom to "acquirer-grade external sprint" at the top, each rung mapped to the Part L Buildability Readiness Ladder (BRL-1 … BRL-9) where the mapping is natural. None of these rungs sells anything; the end-product sale sits beyond them, behind the S2 gate.
  2. The lowest-burn path (CF2.3) — the single ordered route that reaches the end product while the founder personally spends the least and never sells the moat: protect the moat → option / government-funded validation sprint → close S2 (artifact-backed CIPs) → end product sold B2C or to government.

Governing both is one spending rule (CF2.4), carried verbatim and never relaxed: self-fund only $10k–$50k maximum (on moat protection only), then require option money, a government program, or a buyer before any deeper physics validation. The rule is the commercial analogue of the manuscript's fail-closed discipline: just as no candidate self-promotes past a gate it has not cleared (Build-Contract §1.4), no spend self-promotes past the dollar ceiling it has not earned, and no revenue is booked before the end product it would come from exists. Burn that is not backed by option, government, or buyer money is a FORBIDDEN_PROMOTION of cash exactly the way an unbacked CIP is a forbidden promotion of IP (Part L §L1.6).

Honest framing, stated once and binding the whole chapter. This chapter is strategy, not advice. The numbers are FOUNDER ESTIMATES — ranges a founder offered, not market quotes, not projections, not guarantees. There is no near-term product revenue: the end-product line is a future, S2-gated state, and the method is never sold. USPTO statutory fees are factual but must be verified against the current fee schedule before any filing. Attorney and preparation costs are estimates that vary widely with complexity. Nothing here is financial advice and nothing here is legal advice; an attorney decides claim language, priority, inventorship, assignment, and option terms (Part L §L1.5), and a founder's own financial circumstances decide what is prudent to spend.

CF2.1 Why a cash-flow ladder, and why it sits beside the BRL

Part L already carries two ladders: the Buildability Readiness Ladder (BRL-1 … BRL-9), which tracks what has been proven about the physics, and the refined IP ladder (IP-0 … IP-12), which tracks what has been protected, against which artifact. Both are deliberately decoupled from each other (Part L §L0.2). This chapter adds a third, strictly commercial ladder — the cash-flow ladder — and decouples it from the other two in the same spirit, for the same reason: the value of a screening platform that honestly fails candidates is real, sellable, and protectable regardless of whether any candidate ever closes the physics.

The cash-flow ladder answers a question neither of the Part L ladders does: given that the current standing is BRL-2 and the current ceiling is PASS_TOY, how does a founder fund the climb to a sellable end product without first spending money the asset has not yet earned, and without ever selling the moat? The answer the founder gave, and which this chapter formalizes, is that option / government / buyer money funds the physics — not founder savings, and never the sale of the method. You do not raise a physics-sprint war chest from your own pocket, and you do not rent out the screen for cash; you protect the moat cheaply, and only then let an option holder, a government program, or a buyer fund the expensive physics. Each rung is sized so that the next, more expensive rung is reached on someone else's money — the option's, the government's, or the buyer's — and the only revenue the whole sequence ever points at is the B2C-or-government end product, which sits beyond the S2 gate.

The mapping to the BRL is natural but not one-to-one, and it must not be misread as one-to-one. The cash-flow ladder is about what the founder can fund; the BRL is about what has been proven. The two move at different speeds on purpose: a founder can sit at the moat-protection rung while the physics is still pinned at BRL-2 with no candidate sourced. Protecting the moat does not advance the BRL, and it earns no revenue. The BRL only advances when a real closure artifact appears (a SourceMatchReport for BRL-3, the frozen M1_EFT_CANDIDATE predicate for BRL-4), and the entire point of the lowest-burn path is to make sure the money to produce those artifacts — and eventually the end product — arrives from an option / government / buyer before the founder's own savings are exhausted, never from the founder's pocket past the §CF2.4 ceiling and never by selling the moat.

The ladder carries the founder's five goal-tiers exactly, in ascending order of founder cash required. Each rung states: the goal (what the money buys), the founder-estimate cash band, what is actually done at that rung, the funding source that should pay for it (founder savings only up to the §CF2.4 ceiling, and only on moat protection; option / government / buyer money beyond it), and the BRL rung it maps to where natural. Every dollar figure is a FOUNDER ESTIMATE, not a guarantee. No rung sells the method, and no rung earns product revenue — the end-product sale sits beyond the top rung, behind the S2 gate.

How to read this table — three load-bearing facts.

First: the bands climb roughly 5–10× per rung, and the funding source changes underneath them. The ladder is engineered so the expensive physics is paid for by someone with a balance sheet, which is precisely the Part L buyer logic ("a strategic acquirer should option the IP and fund a sprint, not buy a claimed engine," §L0.6) expressed as a cash-flow sequence.

Second: climbing the cash-flow ladder does not climb the BRL, and earns no revenue. CF-R1 through CF-R3 all sit at BRL-2 on the physics ladder — they protect and prepare around a native-geometry method whose best candidate (the worked exemplar G1, MID-METRIC-001) still fails-closed at the source gate (FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC) with an exotic required source (ρ_eff < 0, energy AUDIT, never a clean PASS). The physics only moves at CF-R4/CF-R5, and only if a real closure artifact (a SourceMatchReport; then the full M1_EFT_CANDIDATE predicate) is produced. The end-product revenue exists only after that, sold B2C or to government. A founder at CF-R2 with a fully-protected moat is at BRL-2, not BRL-3 — and the chapter says so plainly so the ladder can never be misread as "the end product is five funded rungs away" or "the moat can be sold for cash."

Third: every rung is honestly toy-ceilinged, and nothing is sold along the way. Nothing the founder does at CF-R1…CF-R5 sells the method, sells a screening service, or claims that any candidate closes. The protected asset at every rung is the moat — the native-geometry method that names where each candidate first fails and that no competitor can practice. The only revenue the whole strategy ever points at is the B2C-or-government end product, gated on S2 — and that is what survives, as option value, even the expected outcome that every candidate fails (Build-Contract §1.6; Part L §L0.6).

CF2.3 The lowest-burn path — the ordered route through the rungs

The five rungs of CF2.2 are amounts; the lowest-burn path is the order in which a founder traverses them so that personal cash outlay is minimized, each expensive step is reached on external money, and the moat is never sold. Carried exactly from the founder's sequencing:

5. Option / acquisition / JV / gov conversion (deal stage) Conversion conversation with the buyer / government BRL-4 → BRL-5; IP-11 (conversion), fired by frozen M1 + accepting hostile review S2 closed + conversion → Stage 6 becomes possible
6. End product sold B2C / government (revenue stage — gated on S2) A finished end product sold to consumers or a government buyer BRL-5+; the buyer purchases the product, never the method — terminal; only reachable after S2 closes; never fired by "promising"

Why this specific order is the lowest-burn order. The path front-loads the cheap, founder-fundable work (Stage 1, CF-R1/CF-R2, inside the §CF2.4 ceiling) — which buys only moat protection, never a product — and pushes the expensive physics (Stage 3, CF-R4/CF-R5) as late as possible and onto external money. The pivot is Stage 2 → Stage 3: the founder's job in Stages 1–2 is to make the funded sprint fundable by an option holder or government — to arrive at the sprint with a protected moat, an IP position, and a frozen milestone predicate the funder can underwrite. The founder never personally funds the $150k–$1.5M physics, and never sells the moat to raise it; the lowest-burn path exists precisely so that money is external. This is the cash-flow image of Part L's option→validate→convert logic (§L0.6): Stage 3 is the funded sprint, Stage 4 is CIP filing rights only if artifacts are produced, Stage 5 is conversion only if the frozen M1 milestone is hit, and Stage 6 — the end-product sale, B2C or government — is reachable only after S2 has closed.

Two disciplines the path carries down from Part L, unweakened.

  • Artifact-backed filing (Stage 4). CIPs are filed only when the corresponding closure artifact exists (Part L operational rule, §L1.6): no source-ledger CIP (IP-2) without a real SourceMatchReport; no observability CIP (IP-4) without a null-controlled signal model; no future physical-embodiment filing (IP-12) without independent lab evidence. Stage 4 of the lowest-burn path is that rule in cash-flow form — the founder spends filing money on a CIP exactly when, and only when, the sprint has produced the artifact that CIP claims. Patents filed premature here are wasted cash, which is why §CF2.5 keeps patent spending on its own short leash.
  • Conversion only on a frozen predicate (Stage 5), and the end product only after S2 (Stage 6). The option/acquisition/JV/government-conversion discussion (IP-11) is fired by the frozen M1_EFT_CANDIDATE predicate being independently confirmed (Part L §L1.7), never by enthusiasm and never by "promising"; and the end-product sale (Stage 6, B2C or government) is reachable only after S2 has closed. There is no route from a "no" node to "acquire a drive" and no route that sells the moat anywhere on this path — every "no" routes back to keep and option the protected native-geometry moat only, whose IP / option value remains real.

CF2.4 The spending rule — the $10k–$50k ceiling, then external money

The single rule that governs the whole chapter, carried verbatim:

Self-fund only $10k–$50k maximum (on moat protection only). Then require option money, a government program, or a buyer before any deeper physics validation — and never fund the venture by selling the method.

Stated as the cash-flow analogue of the manuscript's fail-closed gate:

SPENDING_RULE  CASH_IS_EARNED_BEFORE_IT_IS_PROMOTED:
  founder_self_fund_total ≤ $50k                    # hard ceiling (FOUNDER ESTIMATE); moat protection only
  to advance past CF-R2 (the $10k–$50k rung):
      require( option_money OR government_program OR buyer )
  deeper_physics_validation (CF-R4 / CF-R5, $150k+) :
      funded_by ∈ { option_money, government_program, buyer, outside_capital }  # never founder savings
  the method/moat is NEVER licensed or sold to raise funds   # selling the moat ⇒ FORBIDDEN
  violation ⇒ FORBIDDEN_CASH_PROMOTION              # spending ahead of earned backing is a fail, not a milestone

What the ceiling does. It caps all founder-personal outlay at the CF-R1+CF-R2 band — moat protection only — and forbids the founder from personally funding anything deeper. Concretely: a founder may spend up to $10k–$50k of their own money to protect the moat (CF-R1, CF-R2: provisional, copyright, trade secret), and that is the maximum. Crossing into sprint readiness (CF-R3) requires option money or a government program; crossing into any serious physics validation (CF-R4, CF-R5) requires option money, a government program, or a buyer — never deeper savings, and never the sale of the method. The two physics-validation rungs ($150k–$350k, $500k–$1.5M+) sit above the ceiling by an order of magnitude on purpose: the rule's whole function is to ensure the founder is not the one paying for the dream-test.

Why the rule is the commercial fail-closed discipline. The manuscript's spine is that incompleteness downgrades — a candidate that has not cleared a gate cannot self-promote past it (Build-Contract §1.4; Part L §L1.6 IP_FILING_IS_ARTIFACT_BACKED). The spending rule is the same invariant applied to cash: spend that is not backed by option, government, or buyer money cannot self-promote past the $50k ceiling.* It makes the downside **bounded** — the most the founder can lose on the venture's own terms is the $10k–$50k moat-protection band — and it routes every expensive step onto a counterparty with a balance sheet and a reason to pay (an option holder, a government program, a buyer who wants the option). This is exactly why the Part L ask is option-and-fund, not buy: the founder's cash-flow ladder is built so that the founder can credibly offer* an option-funded sprint without ever having bet the farm on the physics or sold the moat.

The relationship between the ceiling and the BRL. The $50k ceiling lives entirely at BRL-2. Everything a founder can self-fund (CF-R1, CF-R2) protects the existing native-geometry method over the existing negative-control corpus — it protects the BRL-2 asset, it does not advance the physics and it earns no revenue. Advancing to BRL-3 (a sourced toy candidate) and BRL-4 (EFT_CANDIDATE under the frozen milestone) happens at CF-R4/CF-R5, above the ceiling, on external money — and only then can the B2C/government end product become possible. So the rule and the BRL agree on the same boundary from two directions: the founder self-funds protection of the proven asset (BRL-2) and never personally funds the unproven physics (BRL-3+), and never sells the moat to do so.

CF2.5 Patent cash discipline — keep filings cheap and artifact-bound

Patent spend is the one place a bootstrapping founder most easily over-commits cash, so it gets its own short leash, consistent with the artifact-backed-filing rule (Part L §L1.6) and the spending rule above. The statutory fees below are factual but must be verified against the current USPTO fee schedule before filing; the attorney/preparation figures are estimates that vary widely with complexity.

Item Figure (verify before relying) Note
USPTO provisional filing fee — large/regular entity $325 Statutory — verify the current fee schedule before filing.
USPTO provisional filing fee — small entity $130 Statutory — verify the current fee schedule before filing.
USPTO provisional filing fee — micro entity $65 Statutory — verify the current fee schedule before filing. Cheapest if the founder qualifies.
Attorney / preparation for a software provisional ~$6,000 prep + filing/drawing costs (estimate) For software provisionals the attorney/prep cost dominates the statutory fee; complex cases vary widely. Not legal advice.

The discipline, stated as rules a founder can hold.

  • The cheap thing first, immediately, inside the ceiling. IP-0 (lab notebook / hashes) and IP-1 (the base provisional over the current screening platform) are front-loaded in Part L precisely because they establish priority before any physics closes (§L0.2.2). A micro-entity provisional fee is small relative to attorney prep; the founder files the base provisional on the filter that exists today (BRL-1/BRL-2) early, and that filing is comfortably inside the $10k–$50k self-fund ceiling. File the provisional that protects the product you can already sell; do not wait for the physics.
  • The expensive things (CIPs) only when their artifact exists. IP-2…IP-6 are continuations-in-part bound to named closure artifacts (SourceMatchReport, energy audit, null-controlled signal model, digital twin, mission overlay). A founder spends CIP money only when the funded sprint has produced the artifact — never before. This keeps the largest patent outlays off the founder's books and onto the buyer-funded stage (lowest-burn path Stage 5), and it prevents the single most common bootstrap waste: paying attorneys to draft claims around an artifact that does not yet exist.
  • Software copyright and trade secrets are nearly free and protect the BRL-2 asset now. IP-7 (software copyright over the fixed code base) and IP-8 (trade-secret scoring heuristics held unpublished) protect the implementation and the non-published heuristics independently of any physics outcome, at negligible cash cost. For a bootstrapping founder these are high-leverage, low-cash moves that belong inside the self-fund ceiling.

Net patent posture for the founder: one cheap, early, artifact-true base provisional on the filter (inside the ceiling), plus near-free copyright/trade-secret protection of the code and heuristics — and no expensive CIP until a buyer-funded sprint has produced the closure artifact that CIP claims. This is the patent-cash expression of "protect the filter" in the model's four verbs: protect what exists cheaply now, and let the buyer fund the protection of what the sprint produces later.

CF2.6 Putting it together — the model as a funded sequence

The four verbs of the model map cleanly onto the cash-flow ladder, the lowest-burn path, and the spending rule, and that mapping is the entire chapter in one frame:

Model verb Cash-flow rung(s) Lowest-burn stage(s) Funding source BRL standing
Protect the moat (never sold) (IP-0/IP-1/IP-7/IP-8/IP-9) Stage 1 (base provisional + copyright + trade secret over the existing platform) Founder savings — inside the $10k–$50k ceiling (cheap provisional + copyright + trade secret) BRL-2
Hold / mature the IP option value CF-R2 (≤ $50k founder cap) Stage 2 (keep the moat protected and current; no method sold) Inside ceiling — no product revenue exists yet; none is invented here BRL-2
Fund the S2 test toward the end product CF-R3 → CF-R4/CF-R5 ($25k → $1.5M+) Stages 3–6 (option → buyer-funded sprint → CIPs → deal) Option money, a government program, or a buyer — never founder savings past $50k, and never customer/report revenue (that would sell the method) tests for BRL-3 → BRL-4 → BRL-5
Sell the END PRODUCT (B2C / government) gated future state (no near-term revenue) downstream of S2 closing Consumer (B2C) or government buyer purchasing the end product, never the method gated on S2 (HC-02/HC-03) closing

The structural guarantee the chapter inherits from Part L and never weakens: the founder protects the moat (the native-geometry method/system), never sells it, and never invents product revenue that does not exist; only option money, a government program, or a buyer funds the test toward the end product; and the only thing ever sold is the finished end product to a consumer or a government buyer, gated on S2 closing. The expected outcome — that the physics does not close and the founder/acquirer is left owning a rigorous, IP-protected native-geometry method/system as durable option value — is a win, because the protected moat is the durable asset, not a consolation prize (Build-Contract §1.6; Part L §L0.6). The cash-flow ladder is built so that even in that expected outcome, the founder's downside is bounded at the $10k–$50k self-fund ceiling, and the asset that remains is a real, protectable moat — never a method sold to anyone.

CF2.7 Scope boundary (restated, non-negotiable)

This is a commercial bootstrap / cash-flow chapter. It is not a hardware-construction manual, does not advance any physics gate, and crosses none of the BRL beyond the current BRL-2 standing. It does not instruct on building high-energy sources, beam systems, reactors, radiation systems, weaponizable systems, or flight hardware. The manuscript ceiling remains PASS_TOY. Every dollar figure is a FOUNDER ESTIMATE, not a guarantee; USPTO statutory fees must be verified against the current fee schedule before filing; attorney/preparation costs are estimates that vary widely. This chapter is strategy, not financial advice and not legal advice. The thing protected (and never sold) is the moat — the patented native-geometry method/system; the only thing ever sold is the finished end product, B2C or to a government buyer, and that end product is gated on S2 closing and does not exist yet — and there is no route on this ladder from a "no" node to "acquire a drive." One honest line the chapter must never let slip: revenue does not move the physics — and there is no near-term product revenue, none invented here. Protecting the moat buys durable IP / option value and runway, not closure — the worked exemplar G1 still fails-closed at the source gate (FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC, exotic ρ_eff < 0, energy AUDIT) no matter how the IP is protected. Option/government/buyer dollars climb the cash-flow ladder; only a real closure artifact climbs the physics one.

CF3.0 Why a cash chapter sits in front of an 830-page physics document

The technical body of this manuscript (Parts A–K and the Part L buildability ladder) answers a physics-shaped question: where does each candidate metric-interface profile first fail, and what reusable screening / classification / control assets survive regardless? This Part 0 chapter answers a different, prior question that determines whether any of that work ever gets protected or funded: what does it cost, in founder cash, to walk the IP path — and in what order do you spend, so that you never pay for a patent on a thing you have not yet produced?

The thesis of Part 0, carried into every commercial leaf and restated here exactly: do not build a physical device first, and do not sell the method. The native-geometry method/system — the same metric → G_μν → T_eff → NEC/WEC + proper-distance + gate-card engine that the manuscript already runs at BRL-1/BRL-2 — is the protected moat: it is never licensed, never sold as simulation/screening software, and kept inside. The discipline is: protect the moat (never sold), hold its IP / option value, then let option money / a government program / a buyer fund the S2 test toward the end product — which, if S2 closes, is the single thing ever sold, B2C or to a government buyer. CF1 and CF2 establish the moat-vs-end-product split and the cash-flow ladder; CF3 is the protect the moat clause — costed and sequenced — with one absolute: there is no near-term product revenue, and none is invented here.

The reason a physical device is premature is stated by the physics itself and is non-negotiable here: the document's strongest current blocker is source / energy closure (HC-02 / HC-03), and the deepest-surviving exemplar G1 (MID-METRIC-001) fails at exactly those gates — it declares vacuum yet T_eff ≠ 0 (100% source mismatch → FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC), sourced by a negative effective energy density (ρ_eff = −8.038×10⁻⁶ geometrized units, energy gate AUDIT, never a clean PASS). Until a closure artifact exists — a real SourceMatchReport with χ_source < 1, a real energy/exoticity audit, a real null-controlled observable — there is nothing physical to embody and nothing physical to patent. The patent cash discipline is the financial expression of that fact: CIPs fire only when their closure artifact exists, so patent spending tracks artifacts, not hopes.

Boundary, stated once and governing the whole leaf. This chapter discusses fees, sequencing, and spending caps over a simulation/audit asset. It specifies no apparatus and gives no instruction for building high-energy sources, beams, reactors, radiation systems, weaponizable systems, or flight hardware (CONTRACT §4; L9 boundary). It is not legal advice and not financial advice — counsel must decide claim language, priority, inventorship, assignment, option terms, and prosecution; the numbers are the founder's own working estimates and must be checked against current reality before a dollar moves.

CF3.1 The factual layer — USPTO statutory fees (verify the current schedule)

There is exactly one set of numbers in this chapter that is factual rather than estimated: the United States Patent and Trademark Office's statutory provisional-application filing fee, which is tiered by applicant size. As of writing, the provisional filing fee is:

Applicant tier Who qualifies (general) Provisional filing fee (statutory)
Regular / large entity the default; any applicant not qualifying for a reduced tier $325
Small entity generally ≤ 500 employees, meeting USPTO small-entity rules $130
Micro entity small-entity plus income / prior-filing limits under the micro-entity rules $65

These are statutory fees, and they are the only hard numbers in this chapter — but they still carry a mandatory caveat: VERIFY THE CURRENT FEE SCHEDULE before filing. The USPTO adjusts its fee schedule periodically; tier eligibility (especially micro-entity, with its gross-income ceiling and four-prior-applications limit) is a legal determination, not a checkbox; and improperly claiming a reduced tier can have consequences for the resulting patent. Do not rely on the table above as current. Pull the live USPTO fee schedule, and have counsel confirm tier eligibility, before filing anything. This is not legal advice.

The structural point for the cash discipline: the statutory filing fee is the smallest line item in the entire IP path. Even at the regular tier, $325 is a rounding error against the cash-flow ladder of CF1/CF2 (the founder's $10k–$50k self-fund ceiling for protecting the moat — FOUNDER ESTIMATES; recall there is no near-term product revenue, only the gated end-product future state). The provisional fee is not the budget constraint. What dominates the budget — and what the next section costs honestly — is the preparation of a filing worth having.

CF3.2 The estimated layer — attorney / preparation cost dominates a software provisional

A provisional application is only as protective as its disclosure. A bare ansatz dropped into a provisional buys a priority date over almost nothing; a well-drafted provisional that fully describes the screening / classification / control platform — its metric-target functionals, invariant classifiers, source-reconstruction stage, energy diagnostics, gauge/BRST/UV classifiers, gate-card validators, and first-failure reporting — is what actually anchors the later non-provisional and any CIPs. For a software / algorithmic provisional, preparation cost (attorney drafting, figures/drawings, claims scoping) routinely dominates the statutory fee.

Line item Nature FOUNDER ESTIMATE (not a quote)
Statutory provisional filing fee factual (verify current schedule) $65 / $130 / $325 by tier
Attorney preparation for a software provisional estimate ~$6,000 preparation, plus filing + drawing costs
Complex / multi-embodiment software cases estimate vary widely — can substantially exceed the above

Read the asymmetry directly: the government fee is $65–$325; the attorney preparation for a software provisional is on the order of ~$6,000 plus filing and drawing costs, and complex cases vary widely. Preparation is roughly one-to-two orders of magnitude larger than the statutory fee, which is exactly why the naive mental model ("a patent costs a few hundred dollars") is wrong for this asset and why the patent path has to be budgeted and sequenced, not improvised. These are founder estimates, not quotes; actual cost depends on counsel, jurisdiction, the breadth of the disclosure, and how many embodiments the filing must cover. This is not legal or financial advice — get a real engagement quote from real counsel.

The cash-discipline consequence: because preparation dominates, you file the base provisional (IP-1) once, well, over the thing that already exists — the runnable BRL-1/BRL-2 screening platform — and you do not re-pay ~$6k-class preparation costs speculatively for embodiments you have not produced. The CIPs (IP-2…IP-6) each carry their own preparation cost, and the operational rule (CF3.4) ensures you only incur that cost when the corresponding closure artifact exists to disclose. Patent preparation spending is gated by artifacts, the same way physics promotion is gated by gates.

CF3.3 The artifact-backed CIP rule, bound to the IP-0…IP-12 ladder

The IP path of this document is the thirteen-step refined IP ladder IP-0 … IP-12 (Part L, leaf L9), which supersedes the prior eleven-step IP-0 … IP-10 ladder. CF3's job is to overlay cash timing onto that ladder — to say not just which filing fires when, but what each costs and which dollars are committed now versus held until an artifact exists. The ladder partitions cleanly into three cash phases.

IP step Asset Closure artifact / trigger Cash phase FOUNDER-ESTIMATE cash posture
IP-0 lab notebook / hashes immediately (provenance) spend now ~$0 — content hashes + records; founder time only
IP-1 base provisional the runnable screening platform (BRL-1/2) spend now statutory $65–$325 (verify) + ~$6k prep (estimate)
IP-7 software copyright code base fixed spend now nominal registration fee + minimal prep
IP-8 trade secrets scoring heuristics held unpublished spend now ~$0 — confidentiality discipline, not a filing
IP-9 defensive publication the negative-control corpus spend now low — publication / timestamping cost
IP-2 source-ledger CIP a real SourceMatchReport (χ_source<1) hold — artifact-gated per-CIP prep (estimate, ~software-provisional class) iff artifact exists
IP-3 energy / exoticity CIP a real NEC/WEC/SEC/DEC + magnitude audit hold — artifact-gated per-CIP prep iff artifact exists
IP-4 observability CIP a real null-controlled signal model hold — artifact-gated per-CIP prep iff artifact exists
IP-5 control / tolerance CIP a real gate-supervised digital twin hold — artifact-gated per-CIP prep iff artifact exists
IP-6 Mars-overlay CIP a real validity-weighted mission overlay hold — artifact-gated per-CIP prep iff artifact exists
IP-10 acquirer option executed before the sprint buyer-funded option premium (negotiated; not a founder cost)
IP-11 conversion / acquisition M1_EFT_CANDIDATE true + hostile review accepts buyer-funded conversion terms (negotiated)
IP-12 future embodiment filings an independent lab observable exists hold — evidence-gated not fundable until independent evidence exists

Phase 1 — front-loaded, spend now, low total cash (IP-0/IP-1/IP-7/IP-8/IP-9). These protect things that are real now: provenance (hashes), the runnable native-geometry platform (base provisional), the fixed code base (copyright), the non-published scoring heuristics (trade secret), and the validated negative-control corpus (defensive publication, which also blocks competitors from later patenting the obvious failing variants the platform already shows to fail). The only materially-costed item here is IP-1: statutory fee (verify) plus the ~$6k-class preparation estimate. This is the patent spend that the **founder's $10k–$50k self-fund ceiling of CF1/CF2 is meant to cover — front-loaded protection of the moat** is funded from founder savings inside that cap, before any physics closes and before any product revenue exists (there is none near-term).

Phase 2 — artifact-gated CIPs, cash held until the artifact exists (IP-2…IP-6). These are continuation-in-part filings, each bound one-to-one to a closure artifact produced by a Part-L technical program (L1 source, L2/L3 energy, L6 observability, L7 control, L8 mission). No CIP-preparation dollar is spent until the artifact it would disclose actually exists. That is the operational rule (CF3.4), and in cash terms it means: the CIP budget is not committed up front — it is committed only inside (or after) a funded validation sprint, and only for the artifacts actually produced. In the expected outcome (all candidates fail), these dollars are never spent, because the artifacts are never produced — which is correct, not a loss.

Phase 3 — buyer-funded / evidence-gated (IP-10/IP-11/IP-12). The option premium and conversion terms are buyer-side instruments, negotiated, not founder cash. IP-12 (future physical embodiment — the one filing that would read as a patent on an apparatus) is not fundable at all until independent physical evidence — a real lab observable, reproduced — exists. BRL-2 is four rungs below that (the lab-observable proxy is BRL-6, itself gated by an accepted hostile review at BRL-5). There is no founder-cash line for IP-12, by construction, because there is nothing to embody.

CF3.4 The operational rule — no CIP without its closure artifact (the cash firewall)

The artifact-backed CIP rule is carried verbatim from Part L (L9.3) and is the single discipline that keeps the patent spending honest:

CIPs are filed ONLY when the corresponding closure ARTIFACT exists. No source-ledger CIP without a real SourceMatchReport; no observability CIP without a null-controlled signal model; no future physical embodiment filing without independent evidence.

In CF3 terms this is a cash firewall, not merely a filing rule. A motivated founder racing to establish a patent window faces a real temptation: spend the ~$6k-class CIP-preparation cost now, on the expectation that the source match or the energy audit is "almost done." The rule forbids it, and the forbidding is the point — the absence of the artifact is itself the block, not a soft warning. Made executable, the cash gate reads:

SPEND_ON_CIP(slot)  ⟺  artifact(slot) EXISTS and is HASHED   (no artifact ⇒ DO NOT FILE, DO NOT SPEND)
  IP-2  source-ledger CIP     requires  SourceMatchReport(χ_source < 1)        # L1
  IP-3  energy / exoticity CIP requires NEC/WEC/SEC/DEC + magnitude audit       # L2/L3
  IP-4  observability CIP      requires  null-controlled measurement model      # L6
  IP-5  control / tolerance CIP requires gate-supervised digital twin           # L7
  IP-6  Mars-overlay CIP       requires  validity-weighted mission overlay      # L8
  IP-12 embodiment filing      requires  INDEPENDENT lab observable             # BRL-6+
otherwise ⇒ OPERATIONAL_RULE_VIOLATION (file not permitted; dollar not spent)

This couples the patent budget directly to the buildability ladder. IP-2/IP-3 sit at the BRL-3→BRL-4 boundary; IP-4 at BRL-6; IP-5 at BRL-7; IP-6 at BRL-9; IP-12 at BRL-6→BRL-8. Because the document stands at BRL-2, none of these artifacts exists yet, so none of their CIP-preparation dollars is spendable yet. The honest reading against the worked exemplar: G1 fails the source and energy gates (FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC, ρ_eff = −8.038×10⁻⁶, energy AUDIT), so no SourceMatchReport with χ_source < 1 and no clean energy audit exists — therefore IP-2 and IP-3 are not fileable and their preparation cost is not yet incurred. The cash discipline and the physics discipline are the same discipline viewed from two sides: a gate that has not closed is a dollar that is not spent.

IP-12 carries the rule's hardest clause and is the firewall against the document's single most dangerous overclaim. A future physical-embodiment filing — the one that would read as an apparatus patent — may not be filed, and therefore may not be funded, at all until independent physical evidence exists. This is the legal-and-cash expression of the manuscript's PASS_TOY ceiling: there is no patent — and no patent budget — for a thing the document has not, and cannot, demonstrate.

CF3.5 The spending rule — how the cap gates the IP path

The founder's spending rule binds the patent path to the broader cash-flow ladder of CF1/CF2 and is carried exactly:

Self-fund only $10k–$50k maximum, then require option money, a government program, or a buyer before deeper physics validation. (FOUNDER ESTIMATE band, not a guarantee.) No customer/report revenue funds the physics — there is no near-term product revenue, and selling the method to fund the sprint is forbidden.

This single cap is what makes the whole IP path capital-efficient, because it forces the order of spending to track the order of value creation. Mapped onto the cash-flow ladder (all bands are FOUNDER ESTIMATES):

Goal Founder cash needed (FOUNDER ESTIMATE) What the $10k–$50k self-fund cap covers IP steps it funds
Front-loaded moat protection (existing platform) $1k–$10k yes — comfortably inside the cap IP-0, start IP-7/IP-8/IP-9 discipline
Base provisional + copyright/trade-secret over the moat $10k–$50k yes — at/near the cap ceiling IP-1 base provisional (statutory + ~$6k prep), IP-7
Option / buyer / government sprint readiness $25k–$100k partly — crosses the cap; requires option money / a government program / a buyer sets up IP-10 option
Self-funded serious 90-day validation sprint $150k–$350k no — far beyond the cap; do not self-fund would gate IP-2…IP-6 iff artifacts result
acquirer-grade external sprint $500k–$1.5M+ no — buyer/JV/government funded only IP-2…IP-6 CIPs, IP-11 conversion

The rule is a stop-loss on the dream. Everything up to and including the front-loaded patent protection of the moat (IP-0/IP-1/IP-7/IP-8/IP-9) fits inside the $10k–$50k self-fund band. The moment the path would require deeper physics validation — the serious 90-day sprint ($150k–$350k) or an acquirer-grade external sprint ($500k–$1.5M+), the only contexts in which the artifact-gated CIPs IP-2…IP-6 could ever be produced — the rule forbids self-funding and requires option money, a government program, or a buyer first (never customer/report revenue, which would sell the method). In ladder terms: the founder pays to protect the moat; option/government/buyer money pays to test the dream toward the end product. The CIP cash phase (Phase 2 of CF3.3) is structurally a post-cap expenditure — it lives inside a funded sprint, which by the spending rule is not founder cash.

This is why the strategic-acquirer ask (Part L, L9/L10) is option → validate → convert and never buy a claimed engine: the spending rule has already established that the founder does not — and should not — self-fund the validation that would produce the closure artifacts. The buyer funds the sprint (the price of information); the artifacts, if they appear, gate the CIPs; conversion fires only on the frozen M1_EFT_CANDIDATE predicate plus an accepting hostile review — never on "promising." The cap on founder spending and the gate on buyer conversion are the same fail-closed posture applied to two different wallets.

Three properties make this path capital-efficient, and each is a direct consequence of the rules above. First, the largest founder cash item is a one-time well-drafted base provisional (~$6k-class prep + a verified statutory fee), funded by filter revenue, not by debt against a dream.** **Second, every per-CIP preparation dollar is *deferred* behind its closure artifact** — so in the expected "all candidates fail" outcome, the CIP budget is simply never spent, and the founder is left holding a fully-protected *filter* (the screening platform, code, heuristics, and negative-control corpus) at a total founder outlay inside the $10k–$50k band. **Third, the expensive physics validation is *off the founder's balance sheet entirely*** — it is buyer-funded by construction of the spending rule and the option structure, and conversion is gated by a frozen predicate, so the founder never pays $150k–$350k+ to chase a closure artifact that the physics (G1's FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC) says is not yet within reach.

The model, closed. Protect the moat (this chapter: IP-0 hashes, the IP-1 base provisional at statutory + ~$6k prep, IP-7 copyright, IP-8 trade secrets, IP-9 defensive publication — all inside the $10k–$50k self-fund cap, over the existing native-geometry method/system, which is never sold) — hold its IP / option value (no near-term product revenue; the method is never licensed or rented) — then let option money, a government program, or a buyer fund the S2 test toward the end product (the buyer-funded validation sprint, whose artifacts, if they appear, gate the IP-2…IP-6 CIPs, and whose frozen-milestone result, if hit, gates the IP-11 conversion) — and only if S2 closes, sell the end product (B2C or to a government buyer; the buyer purchases the end product, never the method). The patent cash discipline is the hinge on the word protect: you protect the moat, cheaply and now, over things that exist; you do not spend a dollar protecting a drive, because no drive — and no closure artifact for one — exists. None of the above is financial or legal advice; every dollar figure is a founder estimate to be re-checked against real quotes and the live USPTO fee schedule before any money moves.

L0.0 What this chapter is, and why Part L was refreshed

This leaf opens Part L — Buildability & IP Ladder (v2), which replaces the prior Part L in its entirety. The refresh exists because the manuscript itself moved: it now carries a hard PASS_TOY ceiling, a runnable reference implementation, five known-metric self-tests, nine negative controls, a worked exemplar (G1, MID-METRIC-001), textbook warp-baseline cross-checks (G2: Alcubierre / Natário / Van Den Broeck), a no-global-aggregation theorem (G3), a frozen-milestone predicate, a 90-day hostile validation sprint, and an option-to-acquisition decision tree. The prior Part L tracked a named-rung buildability ladder (PASS_TOY → … → MARS_ARCHITECTURE_OPTION) and an eleven-step IP ladder (IP-0 … IP-10). The v2 pack supersedes both with a numbered nine-rung Buildability Readiness Ladder (BRL-1 … BRL-9) and a thirteen-step refined IP ladder (IP-0 … IP-12) in which every CIP is bound to a named closure artifact. This chapter carries the new ladders exactly, maps them onto the closure ladder of Build-Contract §3, and forward-references the v2 Part-L leaves L1–L12 (pack documents 01–12) that expand each program.

Nothing in the refresh raises the ceiling. The current standing is approximately BRL-2 (a runnable engine plus a validated negative-control corpus), and the entire commercial ask is built around testing for — never assuming — BRL-4 (EFT_CANDIDATE under a frozen milestone). The honest one-paragraph version is unchanged from v1 in spirit and sharpened in form: the platform is a discriminator / screening tool, not a Mars spaceship; the expected outcome is still that every candidate fails while the acquirer retains a useful, IP-protected screening platform; and the correct move is to option the IP, fund a frozen 90-day hostile validation sprint, and convert only if BRL-4 is hit.

L0.1 Why Part L exists, and what it refuses to do

Parts A–J do one thing exhaustively: they take a candidate metric-interface excitation profile Ξ_drive(t,x) = {δg_μν, δA_μ^a, δφ^I, δG_μA, δG_AB, state/gauge data}, run it down the ten hard-challenge gates HC-01…HC-10, and emit a status-labeled gate-card naming the earliest gate at which the candidate fails. The terminal result of that whole apparatus — stated plainly in the Part-G worked exemplar G1 (MID-METRIC-001, terminal 2 TOY_TESTED / AUDIT, token TOY_MODEL_EXOTIC) — is that the deepest-surviving candidate in the corpus reaches PASS_TOY on at most a subset of gates and is otherwise unsourced and exotic. That is the intended outcome. The document is a failure-mode engine, and "most modes fail" is the product, not a defect.

Part L answers the one question Parts A–J deliberately do not: given an honest PASS_TOY ceiling, what would have to close — and in what order — before a Mars-transport-scale acquirer could responsibly move from an IP-protected simulation platform toward a Mars-capable spacecraft program? This is a strategic and diligence question, not a physics result. Accordingly the v2 Part L keeps the three disciplines the prior Part L was built on:

  • Part L proves nothing new about the drive. Every rung beyond the current ceiling is described as open work with a named acceptance test, never as an achieved status. No rung in this chapter promotes any candidate above PASS_TOY. The closure ladder's top physics rung, 5 PHYSICAL_CLAIM, remains marked out of scope / not targeted here exactly as in Build-Contract §3.
  • Part L is non-enabling by construction. It is a gap-closure, validation, IP, and diligence roadmap. It contains no instructions for building high-energy sources, beam systems, reactors, radiation systems, weaponizable systems, or flight hardware. Where a rung would otherwise invite a "how to build the wave" reading, the chapter restates the relevant first-failure and downgrades the language to target-profile-with-tolerances, never apparatus.
  • Part L is fail-closed like the rest of the document. Each rung carries an explicit closure criterion (what must be proven to advance) and an explicit first-failure / downgrade token (what happens, and which status token is emitted, if the criterion is not met). A rung whose criterion is unmet does not "stall optimistically"; it downgrades. The ladder can only ever hold or lower a program's standing — never silently promote it. This is the v2-specific discipline the Build Contract enforces: every program rung carries a closure criterion and a first-failure/downgrade token.

A structural fact the reader should hold from the start, because the entire buyer logic depends on it: there is no route from a "no" node to "acquire a drive." Every "no" in the decision tree of §L0.6 routes to continue theory only, keep / option the screening IP, or stop — never to acquisition. The chapter is engineered so that incompleteness downgrades, and so that the worst honest outcome (all candidates fail) is still a defensible commercial position.

L0.2 The two ladders Part L (v2) carries

Part L runs on two parallel, interlocking ladders. The Buildability Readiness Ladder (BRL) tracks technical standing — what has been proven. The refined IP ladder tracks commercial / legal standing — what has been protected, and against which artifact. They are deliberately decoupled: IP can and should advance ahead of physics, because the value of a screening platform that honestly fails candidates is real and patentable regardless of whether any candidate ever closes. That decoupling is the spine of the buyer logic in §L0.6, and it is enforced by an operational rule (§L0.2.3) that forbids filing a CIP before its artifact exists.

L0.2.3 The operational rule (never weaken)

The discipline that makes the IP ladder honest is a single rule, carried verbatim and never relaxed anywhere in v2 Part L:

CIPs are filed ONLY when the corresponding closure artifact exists. No source-ledger CIP without a real SourceMatchReport; no observability CIP without a null-controlled signal model; no future physical-embodiment filing without independent evidence.

This rule is what keeps the IP ladder from becoming a paper claim to a drive. A CIP is a technical disclosure of a real, produced artifact — not a placeholder for a hoped-for one. Concretely: IP-2 cannot be filed until L1's source program emits an actual SourceMatchReport with χ_source < 1; IP-3 cannot be filed until L2's energy program emits an actual NEC/WEC/SEC/DEC + magnitude audit; IP-4 cannot be filed until L6's observability program emits an actual null-controlled measurement model; and IP-12 (future physical embodiment) cannot be filed at all until an independent lab observable exists. The rule is the operational expression of the decoupling in §L0.2: IP advances ahead of physics only as far as a real artifact has been produced, and not one step further.

L0.3 The buildability gap map — what stands between BRL-2 and BRL-4

Each gap is a closure dimension; its current standing is exactly the terminal status the corresponding HC chapter reached; its required closure is the deliverable that would move that dimension forward; and each gap names the IP trigger it fires when (and only when) that closure artifact exists. The two rows that gate everything are source and energy. They are why BRL-3/BRL-4 are hard, and why the No-Global-Aggregation theorem (leaf G3, verified: the local shortening score S_L does not integrate to a global Δt, because arrival time is set by ∫ δN dλ / N² with first-order front/back cancellation and second-order Raychaudhuri sign-definiteness) makes any premature "Mars in days" claim a FAIL_MISSION_OVERCLAIM by construction. The gap map is therefore not a to-do list a single sprint will clear — it is the honest scope of the work that the option in §L0.6 is meant to fund, not assume.

L0.4 The closure sub-ladders Part L (v2) expands — the L1–L12 forward map

The gap map decomposes into a set of self-contained closure programs, each the subject of its own v2 Part-L leaf (the pack documents 01–12). This overview names every program, its closure criterion, its IP trigger, and its first-failure so the reader sees the whole staircase before descending into the detail chapters. None of these programs reaches an in-scope rung past its current standing; each is drawn so that an unmet rung downgrades.

  • L1 — Source-matched mode program (pack doc 02; the strongest current blocker). Object: invert the target metric to its implied stress-energy T_eff = G_μν/(8πG) and match it to a declared source class, scoring the residual mismatch. Closure criterion to leave the toy: a real SourceMatchReport with χ_source < 1, no hard gate failed, energy remaining audit-visible. IP trigger: source-ledger CIP (IP-2), filed iff the report exists. First failure: the first unmatched stress-energy tensor component → FAIL_UNSOURCED_METRIC. Maps to BRL-3 → BRL-4.

  • L2 — Energy / exoticity & magnitude program (pack doc 03). Object: report NEC_min, WEC_min, SEC_min, DEC_margin, violation volume, peak negative energy density, boosted-observer sensitivity, and the energy↔source-mismatch relation. Closure criterion: a bounded energy / exoticity report. Required red flag: if energy is exotic, say so — allowed language is "visible exoticity burden, remains a toy/audit candidate"; the phrase "energy problem solved" is forbidden. IP trigger: energy-diagnostic CIP (IP-3). First failure: FAIL_HIDDEN_EXOTICITY; magnitude breach one gate over → FAIL_BACKREACTION. (G2 anchors the scale honestly: the Alcubierre reference computation E ≈ −5.0×10⁴⁶ J ≈ −0.28 M_⊙ is flagged [REFERENCE COMPUTATION], load-bearing only for sign and ∝ v_s² R² σ scaling.)

  • L3 — Energy / exoticity & magnitude — magnitude tooling. Where L2 reports the signs and conditions, the magnitude tooling reports the burden: violation volume and peak |ρ| with their order-of-magnitude scaling, never an apparatus. Closure criterion: magnitude audit consistent with L2 signs. First failure: an undisclosed magnitude → FAIL_HIDDEN_EXOTICITY. (This program is the natural twin of L2 and shares its IP trigger IP-3.)

  • L4 — UV / quantum / admissibility program (pack doc 04). Object: classify each candidate's UV dependency and quantum status. Closure criterion: a named, independent UV assumption / theorem if any UV input is used, plus BRST/BV closure or an explicit declared boundary for the interacting sector. Binding: the open UV axiom B-UQFC-14-UV-1 is UNADOPTED and Gap-04 is OPEN; it may be named as a dependency but never adopted as a mechanism. IP triggers: UV-boundary CIP and quantum-status CIP. First failure: UV_DELEGATED → FORBIDDEN_PROMOTION (UV) and AUDIT_QUANTUM (interacting quantum sector). Maps toward BRL-4.

  • L5 — EFT backreaction & domain program (pack doc 05). Object: extend the admissibility ratio χ = max(χ_R, χ_K, χ_T, χ_grad) from sampled points to a domain-wide map. Closure criterion: χ_max < 1 over the declared domain, with a cutoff / backreaction map. IP trigger: EFT-margin CIP. First failure: a domain point with χ ≥ 1 → UV_DELEGATED / FAIL_BACKREACTION. Maps toward BRL-4.

  • L6 — Observability & lab-proxy program (pack doc 06). Object: turn an invariant into a measurement model — a candidate must exhibit a target signal, a null signal, a noise model, a detection threshold, a false-positive control, and a named first failure if any is absent. Closure criterion: a null-controlled measurement model. IP trigger: observability CIP (IP-4), filed iff the null-controlled signal model exists. First failure: a signal that is coordinate-only and vanishes in an invariant / tetrad frame → FAIL_COORDINATE_ONLY (the HC-01 guard reused as a measurement gate). Maps to BRL-6.

  • L7 — Control / tolerance & digital-twin program (pack doc 07). Object: track Ξ_target relative to the ship frame, minimise lobe slip, maximise gate margin, and never optimize through a failed hard gate. Closure criterion: a gate-supervised digital twin with physics gates in the objective. IP trigger: control / tolerance CIP (IP-5), filed iff the digital twin exists. Kill condition (the first failure): any controller that achieves a higher shortening score by violating source, energy, causality, gauge, UV, or EFT constraints fails — the abort/downgrade path is mandatory, not optional. Maps to BRL-7.

  • L8 — Mars-mission architecture program (pack doc 08). Object: a validity-weighted overlay of gate status onto a toy trajectory, and an architecture sensitivity study — never a global travel-time claim. No-global-aggregation rule (the binding constraint): one may not claim local S_L > 0 ⇒ global travel time reduced without a theorem and full mission dynamics — and G3 proves the local score does not integrate to a global Δt. Closure criterion: a mission-architecture sensitivity study with the gate-status overlay and watermark. IP trigger: Mars-overlay CIP (IP-6). First failure: any overlay asserting a global travel-time cut → FAIL_MISSION_OVERCLAIM. Maps to BRL-9.

Object: the thirteen-step IP ladder of §L0.2.2, the option structure of §L0.7, and the operational rule of §L0.2.3, stated as strategy, not legal advice. Closure criterion: every CIP bound to its artifact; option fired only by the frozen predicate. First failure: a CIP filed without its artifact → operational-rule violation (rejected).

  • L10 — Strategic-Acquirer build-program decision tree (pack doc 10). Object: the gate-by-gate decision tree of §L0.6 from current asset to a possible acquirer program, with approved and forbidden program names. Closure criterion: every "no" routes to a non-acquisition node. First failure: any branch that routes a "no" to "acquire a drive" → forbidden (there is none). Maps the buyer through BRL-1 → BRL-9.
